title: Text: grep, sed, awk, cut, sort, uniq, pipes and redirection

videos.script: Every command you have run in this course printed text, and you have read all of it with your eyes. This lesson is where you stop doing that. {{eyes}} The idea is one sentence and it is the oldest one in Unix: small programs that read text and write text, joined end to end. One counts. One picks columns. One sorts. One finds. None of them is clever, and joined up they answer questions that would otherwise need a program. {{idea}} Here is the shape of it. Take a web server's log, cut out the column with the status code, sort it, count the runs, and sort by the count. Four commands, one line, and the answer is how many of every kind of response that server gave. Nobody wrote a tool for that question. {{shape}} We start with the plumbing, because two of the three things a program writes to are not the same stream, and the difference is why redirecting output sometimes leaves errors on your screen. Then the tools: grep to find, cut to take columns, sort and uniq which are a pair, wc to count, tr to replace characters, sed to replace patterns, and awk, which is a small programming language you can write on one line. {{tools}} The log in this lesson was written for it — a real one carries real addresses — and every command run against it is real, with the numbers it actually printed. {{data}} {{title}}

One question, asked properly, with nothing invented. The log has twelve hundred lines. The question is: what is slow? {{ask}} First, what does a line look like. head minus one, and there it is: an address, a timestamp, a request in quotes, a status, a size, a user agent in quotes, and a number at the end which is milliseconds. {{look}} Now, is anything slow at all. awk, dollar N F greater than three thousand, and count. The answer is twelve, out of twelve hundred, which is already useful: this is not a machine that is slow, it is a machine with something slow in it. {{count}} Which something. Print the path for those lines, sort, uniq minus c. Twelve of twelve are slash api slash reports. Not most. All of them. And the arithmetic makes it plainer: the whole log averages a hundred and thirty nine milliseconds, and that one endpoint averages four thousand one hundred and forty six. {{which}} And that changes the question from what is slow to what is slow about that endpoint — which this lesson cannot answer, because the answer is in the application. But the four commands took twenty seconds and turned an entire machine into one URL. {{narrow}} Watch what did not happen. Nothing was loaded into anything. No tool was installed. No file was written. The whole investigation was four programs that existed in nineteen seventy nine, joined with three pipes. {{nothing}}

Three things to take out of this lesson. {{three}} The first is the order. Reduce before you decide: grep first to throw away what you do not care about, then cut to keep one column, then sort and uniq to count. Doing it the other way round works and is slower to write and slower to run. {{order}} The second is that sort before uniq is not optional. uniq collapses adjacent duplicates and nothing else — it is not a de-duplicator, it is a run-length counter, and on unsorted input it quietly gives you a wrong answer rather than an error. That is the single most common bug in one-liners and it never announces itself. {{sortuniq}} And the third is to know when to stop. awk will do a great deal, and when you are reaching for a second awk variable and a third condition, the answer is that this has become a program and should be written as one. Which is the next lesson. {{stop}} Lesson nine is bash: variables, conditionals, loops and functions — the point at which the one-liner becomes a file with a name. {{next}}
